name: One for the World (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Moves money: each recipient its donors give to, read live, brings its own countries.
summary: One for the World asks students and young professionals in the US, UK, Canada and Australia to give 1% of their income to charities GiveWell recommends, through chapters at universities and graduate schools and talks at companies; this model covers its year to June 2024 ($758K of its own costs across its US company and UK charity; donors' money passed on is left out). At the defaults it averts about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000: its 166 new pledges and the year's new corporate donors' discounted lifetime giving (at the yearly gift of its active pledgers, on the shared pledge curve lowered for its faster attrition) and the year's one-off gifts, of which it caused about half (its own strict count: 44%), come to about $720K, each dollar valued at its donors' charities (84% to GiveWell's recommended charities), half counted as new money, the next dollar at {{row:marginal_vs_past_average}} of the past average. The money it moves goes almost all to top global-health charities, and it causes about one dollar of discounted giving per dollar it spends. The result moves most with the discount rate, its next-dollar figure, its own count of what it caused and the value of a child's life; no branch is discounted for missing data, since money moved is counted.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

rows.explainer: Donations by its pledgers and other donors in its 2023-2024 year through its platform, workplace giving (Benevity) and the off-platform giving it could trace, rounded in the source. rows.label: Share of its donors' giving that happens only because of One for the World

source.title: One for the World, 2023-2024 Impact Report
source.quote: Move $1.1m in counterfactual donations to GiveWell nonprofits ... $1,107,000 $575,956*
source.note: $575,956 of $1,303,670 moved to GiveWell's charities: 44.2%, by a method it calls 'less of an estimate of our actual counterfactuality and more a measure of what portion of money moved we have high confidence is counterfactual (higher burden of proof)'; it adds that non-respondents 'have perhaps been assigned a lower percentage than they may actually be'. Its older method, applying the average donor's answer to all money, gave 68% in 2021-2022 ('68% of our donors noted that they were not familiar with GiveWell') and about 60% in 2022-2023 ($1,043,363 counterfactual, 2022-2023 report p. 7); it overstated because its largest donors are less often counterfactual.

rows.explainer: Its own effect (the shared rule, facts/meta.json own_effect_share: the organisation's own donor survey where it has one; it handles its non-respondents itself). The rest its donors would have given to GiveWell's charities anyway. 50%: between its stricter 44%, which it calls a floor, and its older method's about 57-60%, which ignored that large donors are less often counterfactual. Low: the shared figure for an organisation without a survey (30%); high: the share its 2023-2024 target implied (61%, $1.1M of $1.8M).

rows.label: Giving in the year that it caused (US$)
rows.explainer: The year's money moved, with unrecorded giving, net of what donors would have given to GiveWell's charities anyway: about $829K.

rows.label: Share of the year's money moved that is pledgers' recurring giving
rows.explainer: Our judgment, anchored on its 2022-2023 goal to 'grow regular giving to $1m of live run rate' (2021-2022 report), about 65% of the $1.55M it moved in 2023-2024, and on its UK charity, where 57 recurring donors give 'roughly £17k annually' of £159K raised (11%). Its 1% Pledge is recurring giving ('pledging now, donating later'); one-off gifts are the rest: corporate one-off donations ($82,922, Impact Report p. 18) and giving-season gifts. The recurring part includes corporate payroll giving ($252,909 of the $335,831 from corporate workplaces, p. 13), which is taken out of the gift per university pledger below. 70% (55 to 85%).

rows.label: Share of its faster attrition's lifetime shortfall that also thins its current book of givers
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the same faster attrition that cuts a new pledge's lifetime giving (own_retention_adj) leaves fewer of the older pledgers giving in 2023-2024, which raises the gift per pledger. Worked on the curve's first-year share: a constant 20% yearly attrition gives 0.41 of the curve's lifetime giving and about 0.81 of its book over nine young cohorts (0.19 of a 0.59 shortfall, 0.32); a constant 15% gives 0.52 and about 0.96 (0.08); with most pledgers three to eight years in, the book thins more. 30% (10 to 50%).

rows.label: Pledgers giving in 2023-2024, on the shared curve at its own retention (pledger-years)
rows.formula: ((pledges_to_date - pledges_to_mid_2020) / recent_cohort_years * (@meta.pledge_recording_floor * recent_cohort_years + (@meta.pledge_recording_first_year - @meta.pledge_recording_floor) * (1 - (1 - @meta.pledge_recording_decay) ^ recent_cohort_years) / @meta.pledge_recording_decay) + pledges_to_mid_2020 / (cohort_years_giving - recent_cohort_years) * (@meta.pledge_recording_floor * (cohort_years_giving - recent_cohort_years) + (@meta.pledge_recording_first_year - @meta.pledge_recording_floor) * ((1 - @meta.pledge_recording_decay) ^ recent_cohort_years - (1 - @meta.pledge_recording_decay) ^ cohort_years_giving) / @meta.pledge_recording_decay)) * (1 - stock_retention_link * (1 - own_retention_adj))
rows.explainer: Each group of cohorts by its published size, at its ages' shares on the shared pledge curve (floor + (first year − floor) × (1 − decay)^t): the 415 or so pledges of 2020-2023 at ages 0 to 2, the 2,498 before at ages 3 to 8; thinned for its own faster attrition by the link above. About {{row:active_pledger_years}} pledgers giving.

rows.label: New 1% Pledges, July 2023 to June 2024

source.title: One for the World, 2023-2024 Impact Report
source.quote: Existing UG Support 117 $628 Existing MBA Support 29 $1,186 Existing Law support 13 $1,099 Existing Med support 2 $4,363 General Referrals* 5 $708
source.note: 117 + 29 + 13 + 2 + 5 = 166 pledges by channel. The chapter page gives '100 pledges made' (p. 8), likely a narrower count; it is the low end.

rows.explainer: The pledges this year's spending brought from its chapters: counted as a flow, each one's future giving by the shared pledge-persistence curve (Convention 3). New corporate donors are their own branch below.

rows.label: Yearly giving of this year's pledges against the average active pledger's
rows.explainer: Our judgment, anchored on its 2019-2020 averages by school ('Average pledge value from Undergraduates was $629/year, versus $1286/year for MBA students and $1528/year for Law students', 2019-2020 Annual Report p. 10) and the mix of its book: 42% of its active donors were graduate students in June 2020 (204 of 489, p. 12). This year's pledges were 27% graduate (44 of 166: MBA, law and medicine, Impact Report p. 22): (0.73 × 629 + 0.27 × about 1,350) against (0.58 × 629 + 0.42 × 1,350) for that book is about 0.88. It says 'newer pledges are giving more' (p. 22), and pay rises over a career: 0.95 (0.8 to 1.3).

rows.label: Years a new pledger can keep giving
rows.explainer: Our judgment: its pledgers are students and young professionals, most in their twenties, who pledge 1% of their income for their working lives; from about 27 to 65 is 38 years. Low: a shorter giving life; high: from 22. The shared persistence curve below decides how many still give.

rows.label: Discounted years of giving per new pledge (share still giving each year, summed)
rows.explainer: The shared pledge-persistence figures (facts/meta.json, from Giving What We Can's cohort data): the share of pledgers giving in year t is floor + (first year − floor) × (1 − decay)^t, each year discounted at the site's rate. The fading part is an annuity at the combined rate (1 + discount) / (1 − decay) − 1. About {{row:pledge_persistence_years}} at 4%; its own pledgers drop out faster (own_retention_adj).

rows.label: Its 1% pledgers' lifetime giving against the shared curve's
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The shared curve, fitted to Giving What We Can's 10% pledgers, keeps about 90% of a young book of givers from year to year and a floor of 28% giving for decades. One for the World's own book keeps less: 64% of donors and 71% of dollars due to start giving did start in 2019-2020 (2019-2020 Annual Report p. 12) and 73% of the run rate due in 2022-2023 (2022-2023 report p. 7); it retained 80% of active donors' yearly giving in 2022-2023 (p. 7); pledge attrition was 'over 20%' in 2023-2024 (p. 4), 16% in 2024-2025 and 12.9% so far in 2025-2026 (EA Forum, November 2025). At 73% activation and 80-87% yearly retention a pledge's discounted lifetime giving is about 0.51-0.72 of the curve's; some of its pledgers will stay for decades as the curve's floor says. 65% (45%: a constant 20% attrition; 100%: the shared curve).

rows.label: Years from a pledge to its first gift
rows.explainer: Our judgment, from its own start dates: of its undergraduate-heavy 2019-2020 cohort, '43% of this recruitment has already come online or is due to within the next year', and most pledgers come online within 12 months of graduation (2019-2020 Annual Report pp. 10-11); 70% of the 2023-2024 pledges came from undergraduate chapters (117 of 166, Impact Report p. 22), while graduate pledgers give at once. About a year and a half (half a year to two and a half).

rows.label: Lifetime giving it caused through the year's new pledges, discounted (US$)
rows.formula: new_pledges * yearly_gift_per_pledger * new_pledge_size_adj * pledge_persistence_years * own_retention_adj * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -activation_wait_years * own_effect
rows.explainer: New pledges × yearly giving × discounted years of giving (the shared curve, at its own retention), after the wait to the first gift, × its own effect: the template's recipe for pledges.

rows.label: Yearly recurring giving of the corporate donors recruited in the year (US$)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: about 20 company talks a year at about $2,800 of new recurring giving per talk, its own average over its first 47 talks ('Totals 47 $134,592 $2,800', EA Forum, 'Lessons and results from workplace giving talks', March 2022, https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/QpAbe8Dqig3o5GPrx). Its 2023-2024 pledge table has no workplace channel, so these recruits are counted here. Low: ten talks; high: twice the talks or the run rate.

rows.label: Lifetime giving it caused through the year's new corporate donors, discounted (US$)
rows.explainer: The year's new corporate run rate over the shared pledge curve, discounted, × its own effect. Working donors give at once (no activation wait). It reports '~100% retention' for them, but over 2 to 17 months only (March 2022 post), so their retention is taken halfway between the shared curve and its university pledgers' (own_retention_adj).

rows.label: One-off giving it caused in the year (US$)
rows.explainer: One-off gifts are a flow already: the year's, against the year's cost.

rows.label: Money moved that it caused (US$)
rows.explainer: This year's university and corporate recruits' discounted lifetime giving and the year's one-off gifts, net of what donors would have given to GiveWell's charities anyway: about $720K. Where it went is in value_destinations; half of it counts as new money, the rest only for the gain over where it would have gone (the shared rows).

rows.label: Money moved it caused per dollar of its own costs
rows.explainer: Context: about one dollar of caused, discounted giving per dollar it spends; its gross yearly ratio of money moved to own costs is about 2.

rows.label: Years donations wait in its accounts before reaching charities
rows.explainer: Our judgment, from its balance sheets: money restricted for its Top Picks rose from $199,126 to $510,515 over the year on $1,024,075 of restricted gifts (audited statements, Note 5), about a third of a year held; the UK charity received £193,460, granted £39,928 and carried £313,977 forward, over a year held. Weighted by the money (about two thirds through the US books, a sixth through the UK, the rest given off its books straight to the charities): about 0.45 years.

rows.label: The wait before donations reach charities, discounted
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: Value of a dollar to global health and poverty charities (GiveWell's Top Charities, live), units of value
rows.explainer: GiveWell's four Top Charities (Against Malaria Foundation, Malaria Consortium, Helen Keller Intl, New Incentives), each at GiveWell's figure for the charity on the rankings (its programmes and locations weighted by funding) under your values, weighted by what GiveWell directed to each in 2024 (50%, 29%, 18%, 4%).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, units of value
rows.explainer: Valued by where this organisation's money went: its own published split, each recipient at its live result on this site (value_destinations).

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Shifted money was going to be given anyway; it is credited only for the gain. Where it would have gone is valued at GiveDirectly's live result (GiveWell's model), as Ambitious Impact does, times a shared multiple (1×, from 0 to 3×).

rows.label: Share of money moved that is new money
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for every meta charity: about half the money moved wouldn't otherwise have been given (Ambitious Impact's Effective Giving Incubation report), from 35% to 80%.

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): the charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work.

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, net of where shifted money would have gone, at the mobiliser's share, units of value
rows.explainer: New money counts in full; shifted money counts for the gain over where it would have gone. The donors gave it, so the organisation is credited its share of that good (mobiliser_share).

rows.label: Value of a dollar to the charities One for the World's donors gave to (its 2023-2024 split, live), units of value
rows.explainer: Where its donors' money went in 2023-2024, each recipient at its figure on the rankings under your values, by the site's rule for a split (normalization.md 2.8). 84% went to charities GiveWell recommends (its 'effective money moved', $1.30M of $1.55M); split as the donations through its own books were (Form 990 Schedule I): $495,387 to GiveWell for its recommended charities and $10,217 through Every.org to them, both at GiveWell's Top Charities (value_global_health), and $162,953 to Against Malaria Foundation at its figure. Gifts made off its books follow the same portfolio (Malaria Consortium, Against Malaria Foundation, Helen Keller Intl, New Incentives and GiveWell's All Grants Fund), so they take the same split. The other 16% went to charities outside GiveWell's list, such as GiveDirectly (Impact Report p. 19), below its own bar: valued as an ordinary charity (the shared prior multiple of GiveDirectly's live result).

rows.label: Value per unit affected per year, in units of value
rows.explainer: Unused: the policy branch is 0 (units_affected_per_year), so this row multiplies nothing. It keeps the template's figure and range (a typical policy win's value and chance from the family's reference classes) only so the canonical row exists; changing it moves no result.

rows.label: Probability the change happens because of this work
rows.explainer: Unused: the policy branch is 0 (units_affected_per_year), so this row multiplies nothing. It keeps the template's figure and range (a typical policy win's value and chance from the family's reference classes) only so the canonical row exists; changing it moves no result.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (Your values → How impact is counted; docs/normalization.md 2.9). Never the charity's or an evaluator's own years.

rows.label: Years from the win until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: Unused: the policy branch is 0 (units_affected_per_year), so the wait discounts nothing. It keeps the template's 1 year (0 to 3, a law passed to the year it applies) only so the canonical row exists; changing it moves no result.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
Expected value of the policy or research (before adjustments)
Side effects of the money moved, as a share of its value
rows.explainer: Good and harm beyond the donations counted: chapter leaders and pledgers who go on to give more, take Giving What We Can's 10% Pledge or move into effective-giving work (its chief operating officer's own path) (positive); a 1% norm that anchors some who would have given more, and volunteers' and donors' attention drawn from other good uses (negative). The shared figure for these effects (facts/meta.json): 5% (−5% to +20%) of the modelled value.

rows.label: Value of the money moved (units of value)
rows.explainer: Money moved, after its wait in the accounts, × the net value of a dollar moved, with the side effects.

rows.label: Careers changed to high-impact work in the year modelled

How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far
rows.explainer: One for the World's own figure (facts/next_dollar.json): {{row:marginal_vs_past_average}} (29–95%). Money is the constraint (about five months of unrestricted reserves in June 2025, a projected $160K deficit for 2025-2026, Open Philanthropy's operating support ended), but the next dollar funds a growth strategy whose early results are mixed, at an organisation that missed most of its own targets in 2022-2024.

rows.label: Volunteer chapter leaders, 2023-2024

source.title: One for the World, 2023-2024 Impact Report

rows.explainer: Students who run its chapters unpaid: 'the backbone of One for the World's programming' (p. 10). Its 2024-2025 Form 990 counts 70 volunteers.

rows.label: Hours a chapter leader gives a year
rows.explainer: Our judgment: tabling at the start of term, two pledge weeks a year and one-on-one conversations (p. 11), with leaders' meetings: a few hours a week over the two pledge seasons. Low: a couple of events a term; high: about three hours a week through the academic year.

rows.label: Value of the chapter leaders' unpaid time (US$)
rows.explainer: Volunteers' hours at the shared value of a US volunteer hour (Convention 2): a resource behind the outcome, not the charity's cost, so it shares the credit with your dollar only with credit by share of resources on.

rows.label: Share of the full cost paid by cash donations
rows.formula: cost_total / (cost_total + if($resource_shares, salary_sacrifice + us_inkind + volunteer_value + money_moved * new_money_share, 0))
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources: staff's forgone pay, the donated legal work, its chapter leaders' unpaid time and the new money its donors gave share the outcome with your dollar.
